patient.chief_complaint: Progressive altered mental status, worsening lower extremity weakness, and recurrent nausea and vomiting over the past 6 months despite treatment for presumed neurosarcoidosis.
patient.history_present_illness: A 31-year-old right-handed Hispanic man presents for neurosurgical evaluation with a 6-month history of progressive cognitive decline, worsening bilateral lower extremity weakness, persistent nausea and vomiting, and recurrent headaches with intermittent dizziness. The patient reports that his symptoms began gradually approximately 6 years ago with intermittent headaches and a single unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure at age 25, which led to initiation of levetiracetam. He was seizure-free for approximately 5 years on this regimen. Over the past year, however, he has experienced an accelerating decline in function. He initially developed progressive difficulty with balance, reporting multiple falls at work and at home, and his wife noted him becoming increasingly forgetful and confused. He also developed numbness and tingling over the right side of his face. Eight months ago, he was evaluated at an outside hospital where hydrocephalus was diagnosed, and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. Despite initial mild improvement following the procedure, his symptoms continued to worsen. Six months ago, an outside neurologist made a presumptive diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis based on imaging findings and mildly elevated inflammatory markers, and he was started on oral prednisone at 60 mg daily with a planned slow taper. He experienced some symptomatic improvement in the first two months, particularly with headache and nausea, but over the subsequent four months his mental status has progressively deteriorated, his lower extremity weakness has worsened to the point that he now requires a walker, and he has lost approximately 15 pounds. His wife also describes new episodes of confusion where he does not recognize familiar surroundings and has difficulty following conversations. He denies fevers, night sweats, skin rashes, joint pains, or respiratory symptoms. He has no history of tuberculosis exposure or travel to endemic areas. His father was diagnosed with sarcoidosis.

mri.impression: Multifocal solid and cystic intracranial lesions involving the right temporal lobe, prepontine cistern, and left cerebellum, with extensive diffuse nodular basimeningeal enhancement. tissue_diagnosis.impression: Integrated diagnosis: Diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2 with leptomeningeal dissemination. The layered report is what the WHO CNS5 classification requires — histology, grade and molecular findings combined — and it is what converts a radiological suspicion into a diagnosis that determines treatment. results.title: Protoplasmic astrocytomas: a review of clinical, radiological and pathological features
results.key_finding: Protoplasmic astrocytomas are rare WHO grade II tumors with distinctive histological features including low cellularity and prominent mucinous microcystic change. They can mimic non-neoplastic lesions on imaging and biopsy, leading to diagnostic delay.

results.title: Leptomeningeal dissemination of low-grade gliomas: systematic review
results.key_finding: Leptomeningeal dissemination occurs in approximately 3-5% of diffuse gliomas, more commonly in high-grade tumors but occasionally in IDH-mutant low-grade astrocytomas. Prognosis with meningeal spread is significantly worse than for localized disease.

results.title: IDH-mutant astrocytomas: molecular classification and treatment implications
results.key_finding: IDH-mutant astrocytomas benefit from maximal safe resection followed by radiation therapy and temozolomide chemotherapy. MGMT methylation predicts better response to temozolomide. Even in the setting of disseminated disease, temozolomide with radiation offers median survival improvements.

output.proposed: Temozolomide 150 mg/m2 for 5 days of 28-day cycle (adjuvant chemotherapy)
interactions: Levetiracetam: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Levetiracetam is a preferred antiepileptic in glioma patients as it does not induce hepatic enzymes.
Prednisone/dexamethasone: Concurrent corticosteroids are commonly used during glioma treatment for edema management. No direct drug interaction but may mask symptoms of tumor progression.
contraindications: Severe myelosuppression: Temozolomide causes dose-limiting thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. Baseline CBC must be checked before each cycle.
warnings: Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is recommended during concurrent temozolomide and radiation due to lymphopenia risk
Monitor CBC weekly during first cycle, then prior to each subsequent cycle
Hepatotoxicity: Monitor liver function tests periodically
Temozolomide bioavailability is reduced by food — administer on empty stomach
output.formulary_status: On formulary, requires neuro-oncology approval for initiation

Lomustine monotherapy — used in recurrent gliomas
Bevacizumab — anti-VEGF therapy for recurrent high-grade gliomas, less evidence in low-grade setting

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging mass effect (effacement of ventricles / sulci / cisterns): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Imaging plans the approach and identifies the enhancing target to sample; biopsying before it risks a non-diagnostic specimen from a necrotic centre

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to control symptomatic peritumoral edema; titrate to lowest effective dose
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of intracranial mass effect — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Tissue diagnosis revealed an IDH-mutant lower-grade astrocytoma — distinct prognosis and treatment from IDH-wildtype GBM
Leptomeningeal dissemination from a parenchymal glioma warrants extended imaging (full-spine MRI) and consideration of adjuvant therapy beyond standard low-grade glioma management
Even for low-grade glioma, pre-operative MRI characterization and multidisciplinary planning are standard before biopsy

metadata.condition_name: Brain tumor — high-grade glioma (astrocytoma with protoplasmic features)
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle due to initial misdiagnosis as neurosarcoidosis, false-negative initial biopsy, partial steroid response mimicking treatment success, family history of sarcoidosis as red herring, and rare tumor subtype with atypical leptomeningeal dissemination pattern
metadata.revision_reason: per-case audit: baseline panels named by an optimal action and absent from the payload actually served (type_and_screen). Reported as unremarkable only after checking that nothing in the case — no abnormal row, no interpretation, no expected_finding, no reasoning — states an abnormality for them
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Off-pathway / atypical tumor histology (the case body diagnosis is not standard IDH-wildtype GBM); 5 required tools, 0 red herring(s); diagnosis requires recognizing mimic imaging patterns and adjusting management accordingly
case_body_concerns: Tissue diagnosis is an IDH-mutant WHO grade-2 astrocytoma with leptomeningeal dissemination — a lower-grade glioma with unusual dissemination pattern, not the high-grade glioma (GBM/anaplastic astrocytoma) that the GLIO-HG pack targets. The workup is similar but treatment intent and prognosis differ. Consider re-filing under a low-grade-glioma or atypical-glioma pack.
